case_analysis.focal_point: Whether New Jersey’s Attorney General may enforce a state investigatory subpoena (and related consumer-protection investigation) against a nonprofit/pregnancy resource center when the recipient alleges the subpoena and investigation chill First Amendment–protected speech and association and seeks federal-court relief before state-court enforcement is final.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (speech, expressive association) and the Fourteenth Amendment (as the vehicle for applying the First Amendment to state officials); procedural/justiciability doctrines governing federal intervention in state proceedings (commonly framed through Younger abstention and related limits on pre-enforcement federal suits); New Jersey consumer-protection investigative authority (e.g., subpoena power under the New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act, as reflected in the referenced Platkin state litigation).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The petitioner (First Choice Women’s Resource Centers) argues that the Attorney General’s subpoena/investigation targets or burdens protected pro-life counseling and donor/supporter relationships, imposing unconstitutional chill on speech and association; because the subpoena operates as an immediate First Amendment injury, the organization should be able to obtain prompt federal judicial review (including injunctive relief) without being forced to endure protracted state subpoena-enforcement processes that functionally suppress advocacy; petitioner-friendly framing in the record also invokes the Supreme Court’s rejection of loose 'prudential standing' labels (Lexmark) to emphasize that threshold dismissals should be treated as proper statutory/cause-of-action or jurisdictional analyses rather than discretionary prudential doctrines.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The respondent (Attorney General Platkin) contends the investigation is a routine, viewpoint-neutral consumer-protection inquiry authorized by state law, and that federal courts should not interfere with ongoing or available state processes for subpoena challenges/enforcement; respondent also maintains that the petitioner can raise constitutional objections in state court, making federal equitable intervention improper under abstention/comity principles and premature because there is no final enforcement action or concrete First Amendment violation beyond ordinary compliance burdens.
key_precedents: Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Platkin v. Smith & Wesson Sales Co., 474 N.J. Super. 476 (App. Div. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point for petitioner: under Sprint, a non-self-executing subpoena is not an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” on the day of filing, so we should not enlarge Younger by imminence or a free-floating comity label. I agree with that doctrinal boundary, but it does not answer the distinct question Justice Jackson presses—whether, as a matter of traditional equitable discretion, a federal court should issue an injunction that preempts the State’s ordinary subpoena-enforcement pathway when that pathway provides prompt judicial review before any contempt or disclosure order. NAACP v. Gallion, while predating Sprint, remains relevant not to expand Younger’s jurisdictional categories, but to confirm equity’s historic reluctance to supervise state investigative demands absent bad faith/harassment or an inadequate state forum—showings not made on this record. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right to take chilling allegations seriously, but without a coercive order or concrete barriers to raising First Amendment defenses in state enforcement, the asserted chill is too contingent to justify federal injunctive interference with an active state investigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that Sprint’s day-of-filing rule forecloses Younger absent a pending state judicial proceeding—does not undermine my view because the decisive constraint here is not an expanded abstention doctrine but the limited scope of traditional equitable relief where state judicial review is imminent and adequate before any coercive order issues. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, a non-self-executing subpoena inflicts no completed constitutional injury because there is no compelled disclosure or contempt sanction until the State seeks enforcement, at which point the recipient can raise its First Amendment objections in court. Justice Kagan’s “present chill” theory does not suffice on this record: unlike NAACP v. Alabama, there is no final disclosure order or showing of bad-faith harassment that would justify extraordinary federal interference with ordinary state investigative tools. Gallion’s comity principle, properly understood as reflecting historic equitable limits rather than a free-floating prudential abstention, remains consistent with Sprint and supports denying pre-enforcement injunctive relief here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Sprint’s day-of-filing framework means Younger is not mechanically triggered by a non-self-executing subpoena, and I accept that much; but that does not compel federal injunctive relief as a matter of traditional equity. As the Chief Justice and Justice Jackson emphasize, the respondent’s subpoena-enforcement pathway provides a prompt, judicial forum for First Amendment objections before any contempt sanction or compelled-disclosure order, which makes this a remedial sequencing problem rather than an abstention end-run. Justice Kagan’s “present chill” theory would, on this record, convert ordinary investigative demands into routine federal supervision absent a showing of bad faith or harassment, a practical consequence our precedents (including Gallion’s comity-informed equity restraint) counsel against. Sprint cabins Younger categories, but it does not expand federal equity into a roving power to halt state investigations at the demand stage when state-court review is imminent and adequate.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that Sprint’s day-of-filing rule means Younger is not automatically triggered by a non-self-executing subpoena, and I agree that we should not smuggle a broader abstention doctrine back in under that label. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Jackson emphasize, this case still turns on equitable sequencing and comity: the State’s subpoena-enforcement route offers an imminent, adequate forum to raise the First Amendment objections before any contempt sanction or compelled-disclosure order, which materially mitigates the claimed chill while avoiding federal supervisory intrusion into an active investigation. Justice Barrett’s concern about immediate associational harm is serious, yet on this record it is not comparable to NAACP v. Alabama’s compelled disclosure order, and there is no showing of bad faith or harassment that would justify the extraordinary step of federal injunctive preemption. Gallion, though pre-Sprint as Justice Kagan notes, reinforces the practical and historic caution against enjoining state investigatory mechanisms where prompt state-court review is available, so I would affirm denial of equitable relief without expanding Younger’s categories.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s sequencing/comity argument is the hardest point: state subpoena-enforcement can provide prompt judicial review before any contempt or compelled disclosure, so federal injunctions risk needless friction. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett emphasize, Sprint’s day-of-filing framework cabins Younger to actually ongoing state judicial proceedings, and treating imminently available enforcement as effectively “ongoing” (even if relabeled “equitable sequencing,” as Justice Jackson would do) functionally recreates a broader abstention regime Sprint rejected. NAACP v. Gallion, invoked by Justices Thomas and Alito, informs remedial caution but cannot supply a free-floating threshold bar where jurisdiction exists and a plausible present First Amendment chilling injury is alleged from the demand itself. The better course is to exercise jurisdiction and address comity through narrow, tailored relief rather than a categorical requirement that speakers await state coercion before obtaining federal review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Jackson’s “equitable sequencing” point is the strongest counter, but I do not think it can do the work they ask without becoming abstention by another name—an atextual, prudential carveout that Sprint was meant to foreclose absent an actually ongoing state judicial proceeding at filing. Justice Thomas’s appeal to historic equity and comity is weighty, yet it proves at most that relief must be modest and non-supervisory; it does not justify a categorical rule that a subpoena recipient must always await a state enforcement action before seeking federal protection for a pleaded, present First Amendment chilling injury. NAACP v. Gallion, which Justices Alito and Jackson invoke, affects my analysis only as a caution about remedy; read as a general comity veto whenever a State could later sue, it would swallow Sprint’s cabined framework and our obligation to exercise jurisdiction. The separation-of-powers-safe path is to take the case and, if the First Amendment claim has merit, craft narrow relief focused on the associational-disclosure demand rather than broadly enjoining the investigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Jackson’s “equitable sequencing” point is the strongest for the respondent: historically, equity is cautious about enjoining state investigative processes when a prompt subpoena-enforcement action will supply judicial review before any coercive order. But in my view their approach, grounded in Gallion as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito invoke it, risks operating as abstention in substance—effectively requiring an enforcement action as a precondition to federal adjudication—despite Sprint’s deliberate cabining of Younger to situations with an actually ongoing state judicial proceeding at filing. Gallion’s comity principle remains relevant to remedy, not to a threshold rule that would routinely force First Amendment challengers to wait for the State to sue; we can respect state interests by tailoring relief narrowly (e.g., limiting any injunction to associational disclosure and avoiding supervision of the broader investigation). On this record, I do not see a historically anchored, administrable equitable rule that justifies dismissing or staying a properly filed federal case absent bad faith but also absent an ongoing proceeding, so I would proceed while emphasizing narrow, non-disruptive relief.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Jackson’s “equitable sequencing” argument has real intuitive appeal, but as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, converting the mere availability of a future enforcement action into a threshold bar would functionally recreate the sort of free-floating, prudential abstention Sprint rejected. Gallion, which Justice Thomas and Justice Alito invoke, predates Sprint’s narrowing and cannot supply a general comity veto untethered to an actually pending state judicial proceeding; at most it informs remedial restraint once jurisdiction is properly exercised. On the merits, I do not accept the premise that there is no present First Amendment injury absent a contempt order—compelled disclosure demands can chill association immediately, and forcing speakers to wait for state-initiated enforcement risks insulating constitutional claims through sequencing. Comity concerns are better handled, as Justice Kagan suggests, by tailoring relief narrowly rather than dismissing or refusing to adjudicate at the threshold.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Sprint cabins Younger and that, at filing, a non-self-executing subpoena is not itself an “ongoing state judicial proceeding,” so we should not relabel imminence as Younger. But Chief Justice Roberts’s remedial sequencing point still persuades me: even with jurisdiction, equity can properly withhold an injunction that would preempt the State’s ordinary enforcement route where that route offers prompt judicial review before contempt or compelled disclosure, consistent with Gallion’s comity principle. Justice Barrett’s chilling-injury concern is real, yet on this record it largely reflects the ordinary burdens of an investigative demand, and the enforcement proceeding can test necessity, narrow scope, and add protections (including sealing) without federal courts supervising investigations in the abstract. Lexmark’s skepticism of “prudential” abstention labels does not move me because this is not a jurisdictional carveout but a traditional equitable judgment about when extraordinary injunctive relief is inappropriate given an adequate and imminent state-court forum.

John Roberts.reasoning: Federal equitable intervention here risks unnecessary friction with state processes and should be avoided absent a clear showing that state courts cannot timely adjudicate the constitutional objections to the subpoena. Even assuming the subpoena imposes some incidental First Amendment burden, the State’s subpoena-enforcement mechanism provides a conventional forum to raise speech and association defenses before any coercive sanctions attach, and our abstention/comity principles counsel restraint where the relief sought would functionally supervise an ongoing or imminently available state judicial proceeding. Consistent with our insistence that Younger and its progeny protect the States’ ability to conduct their own enforcement and adjudicatory functions in the first instance, I would resolve this case narrowly by requiring the petitioner to press its First Amendment arguments in the state subpoena-enforcement action rather than in a pre-enforcement federal suit. NAACP v. Gallion illustrates that, where adequate state-court review is available, federal courts should not short-circuit state processes simply because the party asserts a chilling effect.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution’s text and our longstanding equity practice do not authorize federal courts to interpose themselves in a State’s ongoing (or readily available) subpoena-enforcement process absent extraordinary circumstances; principles of comity and federalism embodied in Younger-type limits counsel restraint where the target can present First Amendment defenses in state court before any contempt or final enforcement. Unlike NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, 357 U.S. 449 (1958), which involved a definitive state-court production order compelling membership disclosure amid a campaign of harassment, this record concerns an investigatory subpoena under state consumer-fraud authority, and any constitutional injury remains contingent until enforcement is ordered. NAACP v. Gallion, 368 U.S. 16 (1961), reflects that federal injunctive relief is improper where state processes are available to adjudicate constitutional objections to investigatory demands. Because the asserted chilling effect is not tied to a final compelled-disclosure order, federal pre-enforcement intervention exceeds Article III’s limited judicial role and undermines States’ primary responsibility to administer their own law.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A state attorney general’s investigatory subpoena issued under the New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act is a routine tool of law enforcement, and federal courts should be reluctant to preemptively enjoin such investigations based on an asserted “chill” that is speculative until a state court compels compliance. Under Younger and its modern restatement in Sprint, federal equitable intervention is inappropriate where the State is pursuing (or is poised to pursue) a coercive civil-enforcement process closely related to its consumer-protection authority and where the subpoena recipient can press First Amendment objections in the state enforcement proceeding. NAACP v. Gallion underscores the strong comity principle that federal courts ordinarily should not halt state officials’ investigative and enforcement efforts when adequate state-court avenues exist to raise constitutional defenses. The practical consequences of allowing immediate federal injunctions against investigatory demands would be to invite broad interference with state consumer-fraud investigations and undermine effective enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention is tightly limited but still applies where the State is pursuing a civil enforcement proceeding or proceedings that are uniquely in aid of the state court’s judicial functions; a subpoena-enforcement process fits that framework once the State seeks judicial compulsion, and federal courts should not short-circuit state mechanisms that can adjudicate First Amendment objections. Middlesex reinforces that abstention is appropriate so long as constitutional claims can be heard in state court and there is no showing of bad faith, harassment, or extraordinary circumstances—mere compliance burdens and generalized “chill” are ordinarily insufficient. NAACP v. Gallion likewise cautions against federal injunctions that halt state investigatory processes absent a clear showing that state courts cannot or will not protect constitutional rights. On this record, the appropriate course is to require the organization to raise its speech and expressive-association defenses in the New Jersey subpoena-enforcement proceedings before obtaining federal equitable relief under the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention is confined to three narrow categories, and a state Attorney General’s non-self-executing investigatory subpoena—without a pending, coercive state-court enforcement proceeding—does not itself amount to an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” that triggers automatic federal abstention. While New Jersey has substantial interests in enforcing its consumer-protection laws, the First Amendment claim here (speech and expressive association) alleges an immediate chilling injury, and federal courts have a “virtually unflagging” obligation to exercise jurisdiction absent a properly defined Younger category or other jurisdictional bar. Consistent with Lexmark’s insistence that threshold dismissals be grounded in actual jurisdictional or cause-of-action limits (not free-floating “prudential” labels), I would allow the federal suit to proceed at least to determine whether the subpoena/investigation impermissibly burdens protected association and speech, subject to tailoring relief to avoid unnecessary disruption of legitimate state investigative functions. The State remains free to seek enforcement in state court, where constitutional defenses can also be raised, but that availability alone does not justify abstention where Sprint’s prerequisites are not met.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Federal courts have a “virtually unflagging obligation” to exercise jurisdiction properly conferred, and abstention is an exception with “strict boundaries.” Sprint Commc’ns, Inc. v. Jacobs, 571 U.S. 69, 77–78 (2013) (quoting Cohens) limits Younger to discrete categories, and a non-self-executing investigatory subpoena—before any final state-court enforcement order—does not fit comfortably within those exceptional circumstances. Where the recipient plausibly alleges present First Amendment injury through chilled speech and expressive association, the federal court should not treat comity as a roving license to dismiss; Lexmark reinforces that threshold barriers must rest on genuine jurisdictional or cause-of-action limits, not freewheeling “prudential” avoidance. Because the subpoena’s compelled disclosures and associated investigation are alleged to burden core First Amendment activity now, the petitioner is entitled to federal adjudication rather than being relegated to prolonged state enforcement proceedings as a precondition to review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention applies only to three narrow categories, and a non-self-enforcing investigative subpoena—absent a pending state-court enforcement action on the day the federal suit is filed—ordinarily does not qualify as a quasi-criminal civil enforcement proceeding or as a proceeding involving orders uniquely in furtherance of the state courts’ judicial functions. The “day-of-filing” rule embedded in Sprint counsels against abstention here because the Attorney General’s investigation, standing alone, is executive activity, and the federal courts have a “virtually unflagging obligation” to exercise jurisdiction where properly invoked (Colo. River). Given the serious First Amendment chilling allegations (speech and expressive association) and the lack of a final state-court enforcement order, federal review is not barred as a matter of comity, though the merits of any First Amendment claim remain to be tested in the ordinary way. NAACP v. Gallion underscores that interference with state processes is disfavored, but Gallion involved an ongoing state enforcement effort; on this record, the better fit is Sprint’s limited abstention framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Federal courts have a “virtually unflagging obligation” to exercise jurisdiction, and Younger abstention applies only to the three limited categories identified in Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, 571 U.S. 69 (2013). A state investigatory subpoena and the availability of later state-court subpoena-enforcement proceedings do not neatly fit Sprint’s categories—especially Category Three, which concerns orders uniquely in furtherance of a state court’s ability to perform its judicial functions—and abstention cannot be expanded beyond those “exceptional” circumstances. Where the recipient plausibly alleges present First Amendment chilling effects on speech and expressive association, the Constitution (U.S. Const. amend. I, applied via the Fourteenth Amendment) supplies a concrete injury sufficient for federal adjudication without requiring the plaintiff to await final state enforcement. Lexmark reinforces that courts should not rely on free-floating “prudential” barriers to jurisdiction, and NAACP v. Gallion underscores that federal courts may intervene when state processes are used in a way that burdens First Amendment rights.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Federal equitable intervention is premature because the subpoena is not self-enforcing and the petitioner can press First Amendment objections through the ordinary state-court subpoena-enforcement process, which provides an adequate forum and preserves procedural fairness. Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention is confined to exceptional categories, but even where abstention is not technically compelled, comity and the practical consequences of federal interference counsel restraint when no final state enforcement order has issued and the alleged injury is largely the ordinary burden of responding to investigative demands. NAACP v. Gallion underscores the Court’s concern with federal disruption of state enforcement mechanisms, particularly where the state process can adjudicate constitutional defenses. The First and Fourteenth Amendments remain fully available as defenses in state court, and nothing in Lexmark alters that jurisdictional and remedial sequencing; it mainly cautions against mislabeling threshold limits rather than expanding federal injunctive power in the face of ongoing state investigative proceedings.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether New Jersey’s Attorney General may enforce and litigate a state-issued investigative subpoena and related proceedings against a nonprofit/pregnancy center while a first-filed federal constitutional challenge is pending, and whether federal courts should intervene to prevent alleged First Amendment harms arising from the state investigation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution First Amendment (speech and associational rights) and Article III standing/cause-of-action principles; (contextually) New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act investigatory/subpoena authority and related state-court subpoena-enforcement procedures.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: First Choice argues that New Jersey’s subpoena-backed investigation—aimed at the center’s speech and counseling about abortion—imposes unconstitutional burdens (including chilling effects) on protected expression and association, and that requiring the center to wait for protracted state subpoena-enforcement litigation before obtaining federal relief effectively denies timely vindication of federal rights; it contends federal courts can and should provide a forum to adjudicate the constitutional challenge notwithstanding parallel state proceedings and that doctrines framed as “prudential standing” should not be used to withhold a statutory/constitutional cause of action when Article III injury exists (invoking Lexmark’s clarification).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General maintains that the subpoena arises from lawful state consumer-protection investigative authority, that the target must raise objections through established state subpoena-enforcement channels (which are adequate to adjudicate constitutional defenses), and that federal intervention is improper where state proceedings are ongoing/first-filed and capable of resolving the dispute; respondent also relies on comity/abstention-type principles and procedural regularity arguments (including that parallel state litigation should not be stayed merely because a federal action was filed).
key_precedents: Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Platkin v. Smith & Wesson Sales, 474 N.J. Super. 476 (App. Div. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is Sprint’s insistence on an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of federal filing, and I agree a non-self-executing subpoena is not, in a literal temporal sense, a pending court case. But their approach risks converting Sprint into a permission slip for broad federal injunctions that preempt the State’s ordinary subpoena-to-enforcement channel—precisely the comity and institutional harm NAACP v. Gallion warned against—by rewarding a “file-first” strategy that functionally disables later state-court coercive proceedings. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, once the State seeks judicial compulsion, the enforcement proceeding supplies an adequate forum for First Amendment objections with appellate review, and absent bad faith or extraordinary circumstances our traditional equitable restraint counsels against federal decrees that supervise or halt that integrated process. Lexmark (as Justice Kagan notes) corrects mislabeling about ‘prudential standing,’ but it does not expand equitable power to enjoin state investigative enforcement mechanisms where narrower, precedent-respecting restraint is available.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan are right that Sprint speaks in terms of an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of the federal filing, and a non-self-executing subpoena is not literally a pending court case. But Sprint’s categories rest on historically rooted limits on federal equitable interference with state coercive processes, and NAACP v. Gallion—emphasized by the Chief Justice—shows that federal injunctions that preempt the State’s subpoena-to-enforcement pathway implicate the same federalism and comity concerns even before a contempt order is sought. Justice Sotomayor’s chilling-effect point is serious, yet under Article III ripeness and traditional equity the proper time to interpose federal relief is when the State invokes judicial compulsion (absent bad faith or extraordinary circumstances), because that enforcement proceeding furnishes an adequate forum for constitutional objections. Lexmark corrects terminology about “prudential standing,” but it does not expand federal jurisdiction or authorize anticipatory injunctions that disable a State’s ordinary mechanisms for obtaining and enforcing compulsory process.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan press the best point for Petitioner: Sprint speaks in categorical terms and typically asks whether there is an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the moment the federal suit is filed, and a non-self-executing subpoena is not literally a docketed case. But I think that reading is too formalistic for the equitable restraint at issue because the injunction sought here would functionally disable the State’s integrated subpoena-to-enforcement mechanism that predictably culminates in a state-court compulsion order—the comity harm NAACP v. Gallion cautions against and that the Chief Justice highlights. Justice Sotomayor’s First Amendment chill concern is serious, yet the ordinary subpoena-enforcement proceeding provides a ready, reviewable forum for those objections, and adopting a “file-first” rule would invite routine federal supervision of state investigations with substantial practical costs. Lexmark, as Justice Kagan notes, rejects free-floating “prudential standing,” but it does not compel federal courts to short-circuit historically grounded equitable limits tied to federalism absent bad faith or extraordinary circumstances.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s comity/workability concern—grounded in NAACP v. Gallion—that a federal injunction could short-circuit the State’s subpoena-to-enforcement pathway is the best argument for Respondent, and I take seriously the risk of federal courts routinely overseeing state investigations. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sprint makes an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of federal filing a gateway requirement for Younger in this context, and a non-self-executing subpoena is not that proceeding; comity alone cannot substitute for Sprint’s categorical limits without reviving the very free-floating abstention Sprint rejected. Justice Barrett’s effort to fit this case within Sprint’s third category stretches “uniquely in furtherance of the state courts’ functions” beyond protecting courts’ own processes (like contempt) to insulating executive investigative demands that may never reach court, while imposing immediate First Amendment chill now. Under a pragmatic lens attentive to access to justice, forcing vulnerable speakers to wait for state coercion to obtain any federal forum is an irreparable harm not justified by an abstention doctrine untethered to Sprint’s threshold predicate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Gallion/comity point is the strongest response: as he and Justice Kavanaugh frame it, an injunction here could practically short-circuit the State’s subpoena-to-enforcement route and invite federal supervision of state investigations. But under Sprint’s deliberately categorical approach—emphasized by Justice Gorsuch—the threshold predicate is an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of federal filing, and a non-self-executing subpoena is not a court proceeding; treating it as one would convert Younger into a free-floating deference regime untethered to Sprint’s limits. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Sprint’s third category reads “uniquely in furtherance of the state courts’ functions” too broadly, because that category protects judicial administration once courts are actually engaged, not executive investigative steps that may never reach court. Comity and equitable discretion can still do work in tailoring relief (and abstention can apply once enforcement is filed), but they cannot substitute for Sprint’s gateway requirement where, as Justice Sotomayor notes, the asserted First Amendment chill is plausibly immediate and irreparable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s comity and workability concerns, echoed by Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on NAACP v. Gallion, identify a real federalism interest—but they do not satisfy Sprint’s gateway requirement of an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time the federal complaint is filed. Gallion involved active state-court litigation, and so supports restraint against federal interference with an existing state forum; it does not authorize treating a non-self-executing executive subpoena as the equivalent of a pending judicial case. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s effort to fold later subpoena-enforcement into Sprint’s third category may describe abstention once a court is actually asked to compel compliance, but it cannot retroactively manufacture the “ongoing” proceeding Younger requires on day one. On my methodology, expanding Younger based on predicted enforcement would convert Sprint’s categorical limits into a free-floating deference to state investigations, untethered to the text and history of our abstention doctrine.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan press the best point for Petitioner: Sprint is categorical and typically requires an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of the federal filing, and a non-self-executing subpoena is not literally a pending case. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the particular injunction sought here would preempt and federally supervise the State’s ordinary subpoena-to-enforcement track in the very way NAACP v. Gallion cautioned against, creating the same comity and institutional harms even if the State has not yet filed an enforcement action. Sprint’s third category recognizes proceedings involving orders in aid of a court’s ability to perform its functions, and once the State seeks compulsion that channel is the designed forum for First Amendment objections with appellate review; a “file-first” federal rule would be practically unworkable and invite routine derailment of state investigations absent bad faith. Lexmark’s rejection of free-floating “prudential standing,” as Justice Kagan notes, does not eliminate historically grounded equitable limits on federal injunctive relief that protect federalism and preserve the state courts’ role in supervising their coercive process.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan press the best point against abstention: Sprint is categorical and generally demands an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of the federal filing, and a non-self-executing subpoena is not literally that. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on NAACP v. Gallion highlights the core equitable/comity problem: the federal injunction sought would preempt the State’s ordinary subpoena-to-enforcement pathway and thereby invite federal supervision over a coercive state-court process that, once invoked, squarely fits Sprint’s third category (orders uniquely in aid of the state courts’ functions). Sprint’s “ongoing” language should not be read so mechanically that it authorizes a “file-first” federal end-run around a readily available state enforcement forum for the very constitutional objections asserted here, absent bad faith or other extraordinary circumstances. Lexmark, as Justice Sotomayor notes, corrects mislabeling of “prudential standing,” but it does not expand federal equitable power to issue anticipatory injunctions that disrupt a State’s judicial enforcement mechanisms.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s Gallion/comity argument is the strongest for Respondent, and I share the institutional concern about federal courts routinely policing state investigations. But Sprint’s framework is a gatekeeping rule, and as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, abstention turns on an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” at the time of the federal filing; a non-self-executing subpoena, without any state-court enforcement action, does not satisfy that predicate and we should not convert Younger into a free-floating deference doctrine. Justice Barrett’s effort to fold subpoena enforcement into Sprint’s third category proves too much here: that category protects proceedings uniquely tied to a court’s internal functions, not an executive investigation that may never be presented to a court. From a procedural-fairness and practical-consequences perspective, requiring speakers to wait for enforcement to litigate compelled disclosure risks irreparable First Amendment chill now, and comity alone cannot justify expanding abstention beyond Sprint’s limits.

John Roberts.reasoning: Federal courts should be hesitant to interpose themselves in the midst of a State’s ordinary subpoena-enforcement process, particularly where the target can raise First Amendment objections as defenses in the State’s judicial enforcement proceeding and obtain appellate review—an approach that preserves comity and avoids unnecessarily broad federal injunctive relief. Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention is limited, but once the State has initiated a judicial subpoena-enforcement action that functions as a civil enforcement proceeding advancing important state interests (here, consumer-protection investigatory authority under New Jersey law), federal intervention is ordinarily unwarranted absent bad faith or extraordinary circumstances. NAACP v. Gallion reflects the Court’s longstanding reluctance to enjoin or derail state investigatory and enforcement mechanisms where state courts provide an adequate forum for federal constitutional claims. Lexmark’s clarification about “prudential” standing does not supply a basis to override these structural principles of federalism and to issue a sweeping federal order halting a state investigation at its outset.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III does not authorize federal courts to supervise or halt a state Attorney General’s investigative tools absent a concrete, ripe injury, and federal equitable power should not be expanded by “prudential” doctrines untethered to the Constitution’s text. Even where First Amendment interests are asserted, principles of comity reflected in Younger v. Harris counsel federal restraint while a State pursues its own subpoena-enforcement process in its courts, which can adjudicate constitutional objections in the first instance. Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs confirms Younger’s application in limited categories, and state subpoena-enforcement proceedings can fall within those exceptional contexts where the State seeks judicial orders in aid of its enforcement authority. Lexmark rejects free-floating “prudential standing,” but it does not create a federal cause of action or dispense with the ripeness and equitable limits that constrain federal intervention here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: New Jersey’s investigative subpoena and any ensuing state-court subpoena-enforcement proceeding are part of the State’s execution of its consumer-protection laws and are the sort of state process federal courts generally should not disrupt when adequate avenues exist to raise constitutional objections in the state forum. Under Younger v. Harris and Sprint Communications, abstention remains appropriate in the limited “exceptional” categories, and subpoena-enforcement proceedings can fit Sprint’s third category as proceedings involving orders uniquely in furtherance of the state court’s ability to perform its judicial functions. Petitioner’s reliance on Lexmark does not change that result: even assuming Article III injury and a valid federal cause of action, comity and the practical consequences of federal interference counsel against enjoining an ongoing, state-supervised investigative mechanism where First Amendment defenses can be litigated there. Allowing targets of state investigations to halt subpoenas simply by filing first in federal court would unduly hamper legitimate law-enforcement and consumer-protection investigations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A subpoena-backed investigation targeting a nonprofit’s counseling and donor/associational information can impose an immediate chilling effect that constitutes a concrete First Amendment injury, and federal courts ordinarily have a “virtually unflagging” obligation to exercise jurisdiction once Article III is satisfied rather than denying a federal forum via mislabeled “prudential” doctrines. Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention is confined to three exceptional categories and generally requires an ongoing state judicial proceeding at the time of the federal filing; a non-self-enforcing investigative subpoena, before any state-court enforcement action is pending, does not fit that framework. Lexmark further cautions against treating merits or cause-of-action limits as “prudential standing,” reinforcing that if the plaintiff plausibly alleges First Amendment injury from state action, the federal court should adjudicate the claim. Given the practical burdens and potential irreparable speech and associational harms to a vulnerable organization, federal intervention to test the subpoena’s constitutionality is warranted rather than forcing prolonged state enforcement litigation as the sole path to relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A non-self-executing investigative subpoena, standing alone, does not create an “ongoing state judicial proceeding” on the federal day of filing, so Younger abstention generally does not apply absent a pending state-court enforcement action. Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger is limited to three exceptional categories, and mere investigatory activity (or later-initiated subpoena-enforcement proceedings) does not comfortably fit those categories in a way that justifies federal noninterference. Given the asserted First Amendment chilling and associational harms from compelled disclosure and investigation, Article III injury is plausibly present, and Lexmark counsels against recasting jurisdictional/cause-of-action limits as “prudential” barriers to reaching the merits. Federal courts therefore should not categorically require the target to await protracted state subpoena-enforcement litigation before obtaining federal constitutional review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A federal court generally has a “virtually unflagging” obligation to exercise the jurisdiction Congress has conferred, and abstention is “exceptional,” not a free-floating prudential power to decline cases presenting Article III injury. Under Sprint Commc’ns, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention extends beyond criminal prosecutions only to narrowly defined categories (notably certain quasi-criminal civil enforcement actions and proceedings uniquely in aid of state courts’ functions), and a non-self-executing investigative subpoena—especially where no state judicial enforcement proceeding was pending on the day the federal suit was filed—does not fit those categories. Lexmark confirms that courts should not repackage merits or cause-of-action limits as “prudential standing” to avoid adjudication where constitutional injury (including chilled First Amendment speech/association) is plausibly alleged. Given the First Amendment sensitivities and the lack of a traditional, pending state proceeding at filing, the federal courts should not categorically stand aside while the State pursues subpoena enforcement that itself inflicts the alleged constitutional harm.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Federal courts ordinarily should not intervene to halt or supervise state investigative subpoena enforcement where the state provides an adequate forum to raise constitutional objections and the dispute is proceeding through established state-court subpoena-enforcement channels, consistent with comity principles reflected in NAACP v. Gallion. Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger applies beyond criminal cases to certain civil enforcement proceedings and to civil proceedings involving orders uniquely in furtherance of the state courts’ ability to perform their judicial functions; state-court subpoena-enforcement proceedings fit comfortably within those categories once underway. Practical workability and institutional concerns also counsel against creating a broad federal “first-filed” rule that would routinely derail state consumer-protection investigations whenever a target files a federal First Amendment suit. Lexmark’s clarification about “prudential standing” does not alter the abstention/comity analysis where Article III injury may exist but equitable relief would improperly intrude on ongoing state judicial processes.

Jacobs, and a state-court subpoena-enforcement action functions as a civil proceeding involving orders “uniquely in furtherance of the state court’s ability to perform [its] judicial functions.” Where the Attorney General is proceeding through state subpoena-enforcement channels that can entertain constitutional objections, comity counsels against federal interference with the state court’s process, consistent with NAACP v. Gallion’s reluctance to enjoin state investigative and enforcement proceedings. Lexmark’s clarification about so-called “prudential standing” does not supply a freestanding basis to halt a state enforcement mechanism when the operative question is abstention/comity and the availability of state-court adjudication of First Amendment defenses. On these premises, the Attorney General may continue litigating enforcement while the federal challenge proceeds, and the federal courts should not intervene to stop the investigation absent extraordinary circumstances.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Federal courts have a “virtually unflagging obligation” to exercise jurisdiction, and parallel state proceedings do not alone justify abstention. Under Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, Younger abstention applies only in narrow categories, and a subpoena-backed investigation and its prospective enforcement litigation—particularly where the asserted injury is ongoing First Amendment chill to speech and association—does not fit neatly within those exceptional categories absent an order “uniquely in furtherance of the state court’s ability to perform [its] judicial functions.” Consistent with Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., courts should not use prudential-standing-like limitations to deny a federal forum where Article III injury from compelled disclosures and chilled advocacy is plausibly alleged. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against forcing a speaker to endure protracted subpoena-enforcement proceedings before obtaining adjudication of a colorable First Amendment claim.
